newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle crew prepares for service call to Hubble.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle crew prepares for service call to Hubble.

text.p: Astronauts early on Wednesday tested the shuttle Discovery's robot arm and other tools for a daring tune-up of the $1.6 billion Hubble Space Telescope to let astronomers take a closer look at the edges of the universe.

Astronaut Steve Hawley, who used the shuttle's robot arm in 1990 to gently lift the Hubble telescope into orbit, slowly cranked the 50-foot (15-metre) arm until it was fully extended to make sure it was working properly. The robot arm is crucial for the astronauts to grapple the telescope and pull it into the shuttle's payload bay for servicing later this week.
"Check out is complete," Hawley told ground controllers, adding that the robot arm appeared to be in good shape.
Hawley, a 45-year-old astrophysicist, returned to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's astronaut corps for this delicate and tricky mission.

Discovery's crew of seven also examined a tool box of special instruments that will be needed to upgrade the Hubble telescope, and checked their space-walking suits as the shuttle chased the Hubble telescope that orbited some 2,800 miles (4,500 km) ahead. The first in a series of four spacewalks to service the telescope was scheduled to begin (n)Thursday evening.
"The mission is going very smoothly so far," said NASA spokesman Steve Nesbit.
The Hubble, designed to remain in orbit for 15 years, was built with handholds for visiting astronauts to use in swapping out and refurbishing components of the observatory.
In charge of the Discovery mission is shuttle commander Ken Bowersox, who will make his second visit to the Hubble telescope.

In 1993, Bowersox piloted a mission which included a record five spacewalks by the crew to correct the telescope's blurry vision. That successful mission captured international attention and enabled the Hubble observatory to begin feeding revolutionary data about the origin and contents of the universe.

During this 10-day servicing mission, the astronauts will install two devices, each the size of a refrigerator. The multipurpose infrared camera and an improved spectrograph will enhance the telescope's view of the universe and help astronomers see celestial objects from farther back in time.
The Hubble will also get a set of new digital tape recorders to replace its old reel-to-reel recorders. Digital recorders have no moving parts to wear out and can store 10 times as much data.

Since it was repaired in 1993, the Hubble telescope has provided scientists with the first conclusive evidence for the existence of huge black holes and discovery of planetary nurseries around stars. The telescope has also collected light emission data from distant galaxies and other evidence that the universe may be much younger than previously thought.
The shuttle Discovery was launched from Kennedy Space Centre in Florida early on Tuesday, the 82nd mission flown since the space shuttle programme began in 1981.
